sections.h2: What makes selling quickly in New Bern different from other coastal towns?
sections.html:
New Bern is a river city with an old core, and that mix drives how a quick sale plays out. Owners of historic or storm-worn houses often hit snags with lenders and inspectors, which is why many look at cash buyers who skip that process.

The Census Bureau puts New Bern at 34,724 people for July 1, 2025, about 3,400 more than its April 2020 estimates base of 31,319. Within the 28.42 square miles of land, density is roughly 1,101 people per square mile. The 2010 census counted 29,524, so the city has added residents in each count since.

The Craven County seat has an unusually older population: 24.5% of residents are 65 or over, and veterans number 3,524. Both facts feed the sale pool. Heirs settling a parent's house and retirees moving closer to family appear often, and each wants a clear closing date.

  • Choose a traditional sale if the house is in good order and you can wait for a buyer's financing.
  • Choose a cash sale if repairs, a tenant, or a tight deadline make that wait costly.
  • Choose an owner-run sale only if you are comfortable handling disclosures and the contract yourself.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about New Bern homes?
sections.html:
Homes that owners live in are worth a median of $240,100 in New Bern over 2020 to 2024, and 59.7% of the city's homes are owner-lived. Those figures cover the whole city, so a downtown cottage or a house on the water will differ.

The 18.8-minute commute is short, which suits a compact town. About 84.6% of residents were in the same house a year earlier. Monthly costs of ownership run $1,504 with a mortgage and $567 without, so carrying an empty house for months is a cost worth counting before you decide how long to wait.

sections.h2: Do historic district rules in New Bern affect a sale?
sections.html:
Yes, when the house stands inside one of the city's historic districts. The City of New Bern requires a Certificate of Appropriateness before any exterior alteration there, and buyers who plan visible changes will need to apply.

City staff can sign off on some work classed as in-kind replacement or minor, while the rest goes before the Historic Preservation Commission. The commission works from the Land Use Ordinance and its Historic District Guidelines, both linked from the city's HPC page, which also lists an application, instructions and a worksheet.

The page adds a note on weather. It says living in an old building in a low-lying, coastal place is hard during severe storms, and it points owners to a state preservation office video on preparing and recovering. A listing that discloses the district and any past storm damage reads as straightforward to buyers.

  • Find out if the parcel is in a district before you price the house.
  • Mention the review requirement to buyers early.
  • Skip costly exterior repairs if you plan an as-is sale.

sections.h2: How does Craven County handle revaluation and the tax bill?
sections.html:
Craven County appraises the parcel, and its tax department says a countywide revaluation for tax year 2028 is under way. The previous one was finished in 2023.

For a seller, the 2028 revaluation is mostly a talking point with buyers. The county's page says a comparable sales search will open in February 2028. Until then, you can ask the tax department for the property card on your parcel.

Statewide rules fill in the rest. Bills come due on September 1 and stay interest-free to the first days of January; after that a charge of two percent applies, then three-fourths of one percent for each month from February. A value dispute goes first to the county's review board, and a further appeal to the Property Tax Commission has a 30-day window after the board mails its ruling.

Ask your closing attorney how this year's bill is divided between you and the buyer, and request a payoff statement before closing day.

sections.h2: What do I pay the register of deeds when I sell?
sections.html:
The seller owes the state excise tax on a deed: one dollar for each $500 of consideration or part of $500. It goes to the Craven County register of deeds before the deed can be recorded.

Filing costs follow one fee schedule across the state. A general document takes $26.00 for up to 15 pages and $4.00 more per extra page. A deed of trust or mortgage takes $64.00 for up to 35 pages plus $4.00 per extra page. Satisfying a paid-off deed of trust is free to record.

Recording also sets priority. A conveyance does not bind lien creditors or later purchasers for value until it is registered in the county of the land, which is why your closing attorney records right after funding. Phone the register of deeds for office hours and e-recording rules.

sections.h2: What should a New Bern owner facing foreclosure know?
sections.html:
Foreclosures in North Carolina run through the clerk of superior court, so a New Bern case sits with the Craven County clerk. The lender files a notice of hearing, and service must happen at least 10 days ahead.

The clerk has to find a valid debt, a default and a right to foreclose. An owner can appeal that finding to a judge within 10 days. Once a sale is reported, upset bids can arrive for ten days; a bid must top the last price by at least 5%, with a $750 minimum raise, and every new bid begins another ten days.

These steps leave room to sell, but the room narrows as they pass. Pay-off before the auction ends the case and keeps any equity. Ask the servicer for the payoff and the clerk for the file before you weigh offers.

sections.h2: What are the first steps to take now?
sections.html:
Pull together the deed, your loan payoff statement and the latest tax bill, then decide how soon you must close.

  • Check whether the address sits in a historic district.
  • Walk the house and note roof, moisture and foundation concerns.
  • Collect two or three written offers and compare what each would leave you after fees.
  • Ask the county assessor whether any homestead exclusion on your parcel ends when you sell.

This page gives general information about New Bern. The county offices can confirm what applies to your parcel.

faqs.q: Can I sell a New Bern house with storm damage?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can take it as-is, and a traditional listing can proceed if you disclose the damage and accept that buyers may ask for credits.

faqs.q: Does New Bern require approval for exterior work in a historic district?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior alterations in its historic districts, though staff can approve minor work.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed excise tax in Craven County?
faqs.a: The seller does. State law has the transferor pay the register of deeds before recording, at one dollar for each $500 of value.

faqs.q: When does Craven County revalue next?
faqs.a: Tax year 2028, according to the county tax department. The last revaluation was completed in 2023.

faqs.q: Can selling stop a foreclosure in New Bern?
faqs.a: Paying off the loan before the auction ends it. After an auction, the ten-day upset bid period applies, so check the case with the clerk first.
